claims.text: Systematically varying annealing temperature and time after solution treatment can control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The phase evolution controlled by annealing especially involves formation of B2 and L12 phases.
Controlling phase evolution through annealing enables tuning of alloy properties.
The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs are as-cast or homogenized and have a predominantly single-phase matrix.
A proposed intervention is post-solution annealing over 700–1200°C for 1–10 hours.
Annealing is to be conducted in an inert atmosphere with controlled quenching or furnace cooling.
Annealing causes precipitation and growth of ordered B2 and L12 phases within an FCC or BCC matrix.
Elevated temperature promotes diffusion-driven segregation and precipitation.
Diffusion-driven segregation and precipitation change equilibrium phase fractions and stabilize ordered domains.
Variation of the annealing schedule will produce observable changes in the fraction and distribution of B2 and L12 phases.
Changes in B2 and L12 phase fraction and distribution will produce measurable differences in hardness and other mechanical properties.
Annealing below 700°C, above 1200°C, or for very short or long times may produce different or incomplete phase evolution and limit microstructural control.
Exact phase fractions and transformation kinetics in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs remain partly uncertain.
X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy can be used to compare phase fractions, microstructures, and precipitate morphology after different annealing schedules.
The hypothesis is falsified if B2/L12 phase fractions show no systematic response to annealing schedule or mechanical properties do not correlate with phase evolution.
